_comment: TIER 1 SPINE — Transaction. Drafted from the measured surplus, not from imagination.
WHAT THE MEASUREMENT SAID, AND WHY IT CHANGES THE SHAPE FROM TIER 0
18,760 harvested rows sit in catalogue/tier1-material/. Median phrase length is FOUR WORDS and
the 90th percentile is EIGHT; 26 rows exceed twelve words. A Tatoeba corpus was expected to
flood this tier with conversational paragraphs and it does not — these are phrases, and the
concern recorded before the build was wrong.
The real constraint is agreement. Of 8,883 distinct captions in the surplus, 317 appear in ten
or more languages and only 66 in seventeen or more. Tier 0's slots were formulaic — hello,
thank you, sorry — so almost every language could fill almost every slot. Tier 1's are
situations, and a phrasebook covers "asking for the bill" more thoroughly than it covers
"reporting a broken leg".
So Tier 1 is LONGER AND HOLEIER than Tier 0 at the same time. That is the honest shape and it
is not a defect to be smoothed over: a hole here says the sources do not have it, which is a
different and more useful thing than a hole nobody can locate.
SLOTS ARE SITUATIONS, NOT DIFFICULTY
Tier 0 is what keeps you from being rude. Tier 1 is what gets you through the counter: the
price, the ticket, the room, the food, the toilet you need in ninety seconds, the person to
call when it goes wrong. Ordered the way the situation happens, because that is the order a
traveller meets it in.
Slot ids are `<group>.<meaning>` with a dot. One was written `food-what-is-this` and is corrected here; a single id in the wrong shape is how a group quietly becomes a category of one.
name: Transaction
intent: Prices, food, tickets, directions, a room — and the toilet, which you will need first and suddenly.

slots.why: Continuing the count.
Five is where most of these languages change to a different counting pattern, and knowing that in advance is the point of learning them in order.
Continuing the count.
Continuing the count.
Counting from one upward in order, because a traveller counts by reciting rather than by arithmetic.
Continuing the count.
Continuing the count.
The first number past the counting pattern in most of these languages.
Continuing the count.
Continuing the count.
Zero is the answer that gets misheard most often, because the word for nothing and the word for a small quantity are often unrelated.

match: could we have the bill please
slots.why: Where the word for bill and the word for receipt are the same word and neither is 'account'.
The alternative to carrying cash, and the question that decides whether you are standing in a queue that moves.

match: too expensive - do you have something cheaper
slots.why: The follow-up that gets a different price rather than just a refusal.
The most useful question in the tier, and the one people are most afraid to ask. It is not rude anywhere.
Worth having even where cards are universal, because it changes what you are offered.

slots.english: It is cheaper in my country.
slots.why: Read as an accusation almost everywhere. Included because knowing that it is an accusation is worth more than being able to say it politely.
Used with the hand gesture that accompanies it. The gesture carries the meaning and the word confirms it.

match: where is an automatic teller machine
where is an automatic teller machine atm
where can i find a cash point / atm
slots.why: Recognising rather than producing it: you will be shown the sign rather than expected to ask.

slots.english: Please change this into local money.
match: can you change money for me
slots.why: The word 'change' means both coins and alteration in several of these languages, and the wrong one is confusing.

match: what is the exchange rate for
slots.why: Often answered by pointing at a board rather than spoken.
Refusing loose coins is often faster and always understood.
The most urgent question in this tier and the one every phrasebook leads with. In several languages the word is the only one a traveller needs for years.

slots.english: Can we have the bill here, please?
slots.why: Sometimes distinct from the shop bill in the same language, and using the wrong one reads as asking to pay before finishing.
The cheapest goodwill available, and in some of these languages the only correct way to receive a dish rather than simply eat it.

match: could i see the menu please
can i look at the menu
can i look at the menu please
can i have a look at the menu
slots.why: One question covers a whole meal. Most phrasebooks waste slots on individual dishes instead.
Saying it once at the start of the trip saves a refusal at the table, where it is awkward for both sides.

match: could i have some water please
slots.why: Refusing the water in a restaurant is a small discourtesy in several of these countries. This is how to ask for some instead.
For a dish whose name you cannot read and have to be told.
Directions given once are frequently misunderstood, and everyone knows it. Asking is not a failure.
Recognised rather than produced.
Recognised rather than produced: you are the one being given directions far more often than giving them.
Recognised rather than produced.

match: excuse me how do i get to
slots.why: Incomplete on its own — a name or a pointing gesture finishes it. That is how it is actually said.

slots.english: I would like to check out, please.
match: i would like to check out
i want to check out please
slots.why: Said the morning before leaving, so the bill is not waiting at the desk while luggage is being gathered.
The opening line at a front desk, and the word that gets you past it is the name on the booking.
A practical English loanword appears in most of these languages, so it is often easier than the local words for it.

Shown with a map or a written address while saying it. 'There' is the word the pages use; 'this address' is in none of them, and a slot phrased from imagination rather than from a caption is a slot that can never be filled.

match: can you call me a taxi
slots.why: Hailed rather than called in most of these countries, but asking produces one more option.

match: how much is a ticket to
slots.why: Ordering the number and the destination together, which is the whole transaction.
Answered by a sign or a display more often than by a person.

slots.english: I am just looking, thank you.
slots.why: Buys the freedom to look without being followed by someone for twenty minutes. Not needed everywhere, and very needed in a few places.

slots.english: Do you have a smaller size?
match: do you have a smaller size
do you have a bigger size
do you have a smaller one
do you have this in a smaller size
slots.why: Clothing sizes are not comparable across countries, so asking beats estimating.
Incomplete until the food or drug is named, which is why it sits beside the food slots.
Short enough to say to anyone, which is the point — a phrase you cannot finish is a phrase that arrives too late.
Asked of a passer-by rather than declared to a driver. The pages carry the question and not the instruction to be driven, which is a different conversation with a different person.
Declares the situation before being asked. Several of these languages change tense or register on the word for injury, and the flat version sounds like a complaint.
The commonest medical need is a specific question answered by a specific place, and the word for it differs from the word for a doctor's surgery in most of these languages.
Out loud and to a person, not shouted generally. Several of these languages treat it as an accusation, so it is a sentence to use deliberately.
Changes how the next thirty seconds go. Two words, and in several of these languages it reaches a different set of responses than a request would.
Said firmly and quietly. Raising the volume is what turns it from a boundary into an incident in several of these cultures.
Asking a passer-by for help is a separate skill from reading a sign, and it uses different vocabulary in every one of these languages.
The most common thing a traveller needs that a phone provides, and asking a stranger for it is usually granted.

match: i want to call the police
slots.why: Usually needs a phone, and in most places a local number rather than an international one.
Loud, and aimed at a crowd rather than at one person. Included because the vocabulary exists and because it is the sentence that makes people nearby move.

_dropped: THIRTEEN SLOTS REMOVED BEFORE SHIPPING — measurement, not taste.
Each was written, measured at 0 of 20 languages, and then deleted. What the surplus actually
contains for each is recorded so the same slot is not re-proposed from memory later:
count.how-many        only 'how many pieces of LUGGAGE are you checking in' — one airport
money.not-enough      only 'i don't have enough money to buy WHAT I WANT' — Tatoeba chatter
toilet.nowhere        no caption of any kind; the phrase was manufactured, not found
food.order            only 'i would like to EAT SOMETHING' — a different meaning
food.vegetarian-eats  only "i'm a vegetarian", which is food.no-meat and already claimed
way.write-it          nothing; nearest is about not writing PASSWORDS down
stay.name-on-booking  nothing; word overlap proposes 'AM I UNDER ARREST'
stay.key              only 'i have LOST my key' — the opposite meaning
stay.extra-night      only 'one more PLEASE' and 'one more TOWEL'
move.bus              only 'is there a bus that goes to THE MALL'
shop.try-on           nothing; word overlap proposes the single word 'may'
shop.much             nothing; only 'yesterday I ATE too much'
health.pain           only 'if your TOOTH hurts you should see a dentist'
Two of these are worth writing down twice. A keyword matcher proposed 'am I under arrest' for
"The booking is under" and 'okay I'll take it' for "Please take me to this address" — both
confident, both wrong, both native-speaker sentences. Every one of these thirteen was decided by
reading the caption, not by scoring it. A second matcher built on word overlap would have shipped
nine of them.
Two slots were REWRITTEN rather than dropped, because a real caption exists for a nearby meaning
and the honest move is to describe what the sources actually have:
move.destination  -> 'Please take me there.'            ('take me there please', 12/20)
health.hospital   -> 'Where is the nearest hospital?'    ('where is the hospital', 11/20)
The original wordings — 'this address' — are in no phrasebook. Neither concept is wrong; the
address is shown, not said.
